title: Abuse, DDoS, bots and privacy
scopeHtml: Scope: WAF, rate limits, DDoS defence, bot handling, GDPR basics, PII handling. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: The abuse landscape
notes.html:
Any public endpoint will be abused: by scrapers, credential-stuffers, spammers, fraudsters and floods. Abuse is not a bug in your code, it is the normal behaviour of an open internet, so protection belongs in the design.

Main types and what they target:

  • Volumetric DDoS (L3/L4): saturate bandwidth (SYN floods, UDP amplification). Needs a big network to absorb.
  • Application-layer DDoS (L7): many valid-looking HTTP requests to expensive endpoints (search, login).
  • Credential stuffing: reuse leaked username/password pairs from other sites against your login.
  • Scraping and inventory hoarding: bots copy content or buy all tickets.
  • Spam / fake accounts / promo abuse: free-trial farming, referral fraud.
  • Enumeration: walking ids or probing "does this email exist?".

Worked example. Normal traffic is 2k requests/s. An L7 attacker sends 200k requests/s to /search, which costs 20 ms of DB time each. That needs 4,000 DB-cores of work; you would fall over in seconds. The CDN cache, a rate limit, and a bot challenge on /search cut it to near zero.

Industry examples. GitHub survived a 1.35 Tbps memcached-amplification DDoS in 2018 using Akamai Prophylexic; Cloudflare reported attacks above 70 million requests/s in 2023 (HTTP/2 rapid reset, confirm exact figures); Ticketmaster fights scalper bots daily; Twitter and Reddit rate-limit scrapers.

Decision gravity. Buying DDoS protection (CDN/cloud shield) is reversible and cheap compared with building capacity. Designing public endpoints to be cheap or cacheable is a one-way architectural advantage.

Everyday analogy. A shop front: fences and bouncers outside, a ticket counter inside, and a cashier who can refuse a customer who orders absurdly.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "add more servers"; attackers outspend you.
  • Treating only DDoS as abuse and ignoring slow "legit-looking" abuse such as scraping.

notes.title: Rate limiting algorithms
notes.html:
A rate limiter caps how many requests a key (IP, user, API key, tenant) can make in a window. It protects fairness, cost and stability.

Algorithms:

  • Fixed window: count per minute. Simple, but allows a burst of 2x at the boundary (100 at 12:00:59, 100 at 12:01:00).
  • Sliding window log: store timestamps; exact, but memory heavy.
  • Sliding window counter: weighted blend of current and previous window; good, cheap approximation.
  • Token bucket: bucket of capacity B refilled at R tokens/s; each request takes one. Allows bursts up to B, average R. The most common choice (AWS API Gateway, Stripe).
  • Leaky bucket: requests drain at a constant rate; smooths output (queue-like).
  • Concurrency limit: cap in-flight requests (good for expensive work).
-- Redis Lua: atomic token bucket (KEYS[1]=key, ARGV: rate, capacity, now, cost)
local d = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 't', 'ts')
local t = tonumber(d[1]) or ARGV[2]
local ts = tonumber(d[2]) or ARGV[3]
t = math.min(ARGV[2], t + (ARGV[3]-ts) * ARGV[1])
if t < tonumber(ARGV[4]) then return 0 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 't', t-ARGV[4], 'ts', ARGV[3])
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 120)
return 1

Worked example. 5M users, limit 100 requests/min each. State per key: 16 B key + 16 B value = about 50 B with overhead, so 5M x 50 B = 250 MB, one Redis node. Rate-limit checks at 100k/s need 100k Redis ops/s, and so a cluster or local in-memory counters synced periodically at larger scale.

Industry examples. Stripe uses token buckets with several limiter types (request rate, concurrency, load shedding for non-critical traffic); GitHub API 5,000 requests/hour/user with X-RateLimit-* headers; Envoy has a global rate limit service; Nginx limit_req is leaky bucket.

Decision gravity. Algorithm and key choice are reversible. The big call is where: edge (cheap, coarse, protects everything) vs per-service (fine-grained, needs shared state). Also fail-open vs fail-closed when Redis is down: most choose fail-open for general APIs and fail-closed for login.

Everyday analogy. A bucket that fills with tickets at a steady drip; you can spend a handful at once, but not forever.

Common interview traps.

  • Race conditions with GET then SET (use Lua or INCR atomically).
  • Limiting only by IP (NAT'd offices and mobile carriers share IPs; botnets rotate them). Combine IP, account, device and API key.
  • Returning 500 instead of 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After.

notes.title: Distributed rate limiting and load shedding
notes.html:
With many gateway nodes, a limit must be enforced globally or approximately. Three patterns:

  1. Central store (Redis): exact, adds about 1 ms and a dependency.
  2. Local limits divided by N: each of N nodes gets limit/N. No network, but unfair when load is skewed.
  3. Gossip / periodic sync (approximate): each node counts locally and reports every 100 ms. Fast and mostly correct.

Load shedding is the last line: when the server is overloaded (CPU above 85%, queue deep), reject low-priority requests early with 503 instead of timing out everything. Prioritise: health checks and payments over analytics and search.

limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=api:10m rate=10r/s;   # 10m holds about 160k IPs
server { location /api/ { limit_req zone=api burst=20 nodelay; limit_req_status 429; } }

Worked example. 20 gateways, limit 1,000 req/min/user. Local-divided: 50 each. A user whose traffic hits only 2 gateways is capped at 100/min, not 1,000, a clear unfairness. Use sticky hashing by user to one gateway, or the Redis approach.

Industry examples. Netflix concurrency-limits library and Zuul adaptive shedding; Google SRE "criticality" labels for shedding; Stripe load shedder reserves capacity for critical requests; Cloudflare rate limiting at the edge.

Decision gravity. Shedding policy is reversible config; building it from day one avoids cascading failure (retry storms turn a blip into an outage).

Everyday analogy. A nightclub at capacity: VIPs and staff go in, the rest wait outside rather than packing the room until nobody can dance.

Common interview traps.

  • Clients retrying instantly on 429 and amplifying load. Specify exponential backoff with jitter.
  • No separate quotas for abusive tenants vs normal ones.

notes.title: DDoS defence
notes.html:
Absorb at the edge, filter bad traffic early, and make the origin hard to reach and cheap to serve.

Layers:

  • Anycast CDN / scrubbing network (Cloudflare, Akamai, AWS Shield/CloudFront, Google Cloud Armor): one IP announced from 200+ locations, so an attack spreads across the globe and each site absorbs a slice. Capacity: multi-Tbps.
  • L3/L4: SYN cookies, ingress filtering, drop UDP you do not use, never expose amplifiable services (open DNS resolvers, memcached on UDP).
  • L7: cache aggressively, rate limit per IP and per fingerprint, challenge suspicious clients, protect expensive endpoints, set short timeouts (Slowloris defence).
  • Origin protection: firewall the origin to accept only CDN IP ranges (or private link), so attackers cannot bypass the shield.
  • Autoscale carefully with a budget cap; otherwise attackers inflate your cloud bill (economic DoS).

Worked example. A 500 Gbps UDP flood against a 10 Gbps origin link is dead on arrival; against an anycast network with 200 Tbps total capacity across 300 sites it is about 1.7 Gbps per site (assuming even spread), invisible. Page that is cacheable for 10 s turns 200k requests/s into 1 origin request per edge per 10 s.

Industry examples. GitHub 2018 (1.35 Tbps, mitigated by pushing traffic to scrubbers within 10 min); Dyn 2016 (Mirai botnet of IoT cameras took down Twitter, Netflix and Spotify DNS); Google Cloud Armor blocked a 398M requests/s attack in 2023 (rapid reset).

Decision gravity. Hiding the origin IP is an early, one-time choice; if the origin IP ever leaks you may need to renumber. Multi-provider DNS (so one DNS provider is not a single point of failure, the Dyn lesson) is cheap insurance.

Everyday analogy. A stadium with many gates, outer security lines, and VIP entrances only staff know; a mob cannot all push through one door.

Common interview traps.

  • Scaling the origin instead of putting a shield in front.
  • Leaving the origin reachable directly by IP.
  • Forgetting DNS as a target and as a single point of failure.

notes.title: WAF: web application firewall
notes.html:
A WAF inspects HTTP requests and blocks known-bad patterns (SQL injection, XSS, path traversal, bad bots) before they hit your app. It works at L7, usually as part of the CDN or load balancer.

Mechanism: rule sets (OWASP Core Rule Set, AWS Managed Rules, Cloudflare Managed), each rule scores or blocks requests that match signatures (' OR 1=1--, ../../etc/passwd, known scanner user agents). Modes: detect/log only first, then block. Add custom rules: geo blocks, IP reputation, rate-based rules, "block POST /login without a valid header". Virtual patching: block an exploit for a fresh CVE in hours while the real fix goes through your release cycle.

{
  "Name": "login-rate",
  "Statement": {"RateBasedStatement": {"Limit": 100, "AggregateKeyType": "IP"}},
  "Action": {"Block": {}},
  "VisibilityConfig": {"SampledRequestsEnabled": true}
}

Worked example. Rolling out: week 1 run OWASP CRS in log-only, 0.4% of legitimate requests flag (false positives, for example a rich-text editor posting <script> samples); tune exclusions; week 2 enable blocking for the high-confidence rules; keep sampling to find drift. Adds about 1 to 5 ms of latency.

Industry examples. AWS WAF (used with CloudFront/ALB), Cloudflare WAF, ModSecurity with OWASP CRS on Nginx, Akamai Kona. Capital One 2019 showed WAFs do not fix over-privileged internal roles.

Decision gravity. A WAF is reversible and quick to deploy. Danger: a false-positive rule blocking real customers silently. It is a safety net, not a substitute for input validation and patching.

Everyday analogy. An airport scanner that looks at every bag for known dangerous items; it will miss novel threats and occasionally flags a harmless bag.

Common interview traps.

  • "We have a WAF so injection is solved."
  • Going straight to block mode without a log-only period.
  • Not inspecting what the WAF cannot see (E2EE or encrypted payloads, gRPC/binary bodies).

notes.title: Bot detection and mitigation
notes.html:
Bots are automated clients; some are good (Googlebot), many are not. The goal is to make abuse expensive, not to block all automation.

Signals, cheap to costly:

  1. Reputation: IP ranges of data centers and VPN/proxy services, known bad ASNs, threat feeds.
  2. Behaviour: request rate, no cookies, perfectly regular timing, sequential id walking, no mouse/touch events.
  3. Fingerprinting: TLS fingerprint (JA3/JA4), HTTP/2 settings, header order, browser/device attributes.
  4. Challenges: JavaScript proof-of-work, CAPTCHA (reCAPTCHA, hCaptcha, Cloudflare Turnstile), mobile attestation (Play Integrity, Apple App Attest).
  5. Business logic: per-account limits, purchase limits, queueing (virtual waiting room), step-up MFA, honeypot fields, one-time tokens.

Combine into a risk score and respond in tiers: allow, throttle, challenge, block, or tarpit.

Worked example. Sneaker drop: 1M real users, 5M bot requests for 10k pairs. Virtual waiting room admits 2k users/min in random order, per-account purchase limit 1, one card per order, challenge only on suspicious scores. Real users see a queue; bots lose their speed advantage.

Industry examples. Cloudflare Bot Management, Akamai, DataDome, PerimeterX; Ticketmaster Verified Fan; Google Play Integrity for Android apps; Instagram and LinkedIn aggressively detect scrapers. Well-behaved crawlers are verified by reverse DNS and robots.txt obeyed.

Decision gravity. It is an arms race; build it as a replaceable layer with tunable rules. Over-aggressive blocking hurts conversion and accessibility (CAPTCHAs are a barrier).

Everyday analogy. A shop that notices someone filling a trolley with 200 identical items and asks for ID and a limit, while greeting normal shoppers as usual.

Common interview traps.

  • Relying only on IP blocks.
  • CAPTCHA everywhere (poor UX, and solvable by farms for about $1 per 1,000).
  • Ignoring mobile apps: attestation, not CAPTCHA, is the right tool there.

notes.title: Account abuse: credential stuffing and fraud
notes.html:
Credential stuffing tries billions of leaked pairs; even a 0.1% hit rate yields many accounts. Defences must work at login and after.

Controls:

  • Per-IP and per-account limits, with exponential backoff; do not hard-lock accounts (attackers could lock out victims); soft-lock with step-up verification.
  • Breached-password checks (k-anonymity API of Have I Been Pwned), MFA / passkeys, new-device and impossible-travel checks.
  • Uniform responses: same message and timing for "unknown user" vs "wrong password" to prevent enumeration.
  • Risk-based auth: low risk flows straight through; high risk (new country, Tor) adds OTP.
  • Fraud signals: device id, velocity (cards per account per hour), email domain reputation, disposable email lists.

Worked example. Attacker has 10M leaked pairs, rotating 100k IPs; each IP does 100 tries/day. Per-IP limits barely help. A per-account limit of 5 failures/hour plus an IP reputation score plus a device cookie cuts successful takeovers from about 0.5% of tries (50k accounts) to under 1,000.

Industry examples. Netflix, Disney+ and Spotify credential-stuffing waves; Okta "Credential Stuffing" detections; Stripe Radar (ML scoring each charge); Uber and Swiggy promo-code fraud rules; Paytm and PhonePe velocity checks.

Decision gravity. Fraud systems are reversible and iterative; the hard-to-reverse decision is logging enough signals (device, IP, timing) from the start to feed ML later.

Everyday analogy. A bank teller who remembers you; unusual behaviour (a new city and a huge withdrawal) triggers extra questions.

Common interview traps.

  • Account lockout as the only control (denial of service on victims).
  • Different error messages that reveal whether the account exists.

notes.title: GDPR basics
notes.html:
GDPR is the EU law giving people control over their personal data; it applies to anyone handling EU residents' data, wherever the company is. Fines up to 4% of global annual turnover or 20M euros, whichever is higher.

Core ideas for engineers:

  • Lawful basis for processing (consent, contract, legitimate interest, legal obligation).
  • Data subject rights: access (give a copy), rectification, erasure ("right to be forgotten"), portability (machine-readable export), objection, restriction.
  • Data minimisation and purpose limitation: collect only what you need, use it only for the stated reason.
  • Storage limitation: retention periods; delete when no longer needed.
  • Security (Article 32) and breach notification within 72 hours to the regulator.
  • Privacy by design/default, DPIA for risky processing, DPO where required.
  • Cross-border transfers: need safeguards (SCCs, adequacy decisions); data residency is often required in design (EU data stays in EU regions).
  • Similar laws: CCPA/CPRA (California), DPDP Act 2023 (India), LGPD (Brazil). Confirm legal details with counsel.

Worked example. Erasure request for user 42: 12 systems hold data (OLTP DB, search index, caches, warehouse, S3 logs, backups, analytics vendor, support tool). SLA: complete within 30 days. Design: one user_id key everywhere, a deletion event consumed by each system, a ledger proving completion. Backups: either wait for natural expiry (documented, for example 35 days) or crypto-shred.

Industry examples. Meta fined 1.2B euros (2023) for transfers to the US; Amazon 746M euros (2021); Google and Apple provide data export tools ("Takeout", privacy portal); Spotify and Airbnb run deletion pipelines driven by events.

Decision gravity. Retrofitting erasure into a system with copied data everywhere is a very expensive one-way mess. Designing data lineage and a single subject identifier early is cheap.

Everyday analogy. A library that must show you every card it has on you, correct it, and destroy it on request, including the copies in the back room.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting backups, logs, caches and analytics copies in an erasure design.
  • Hard-deleting rows that other legal rules (tax records) require you to keep: erasure has exceptions.
  • Treating GDPR as legal-only; it dictates architecture (residency, retention, consent storage).

notes.title: PII handling and data classification
notes.html:
PII (personally identifiable information) is anything that identifies a person: name, email, phone, address, IP, device id, government id, biometrics, location. Handle it with the fewest copies, the shortest life and the tightest access.

Practices:

  • Classify data: public, internal, confidential, restricted (PII, payment, health). Tag columns and fields.
  • Minimise and isolate: keep PII in one service/DB (a "PII vault"); other systems store an opaque user_id or token.
  • Tokenisation vs pseudonymisation vs anonymisation: tokens map back via the vault; pseudonymised data is still personal data under GDPR; truly anonymised data (not re-identifiable) is out of scope but hard to achieve.
  • Mask in non-prod and logs: a***@gmail.com, last 4 digits; never copy prod PII into staging.
  • Access control + audit: just-in-time access, every read logged; column-level encryption for the most sensitive fields.
  • Retention jobs: TTL deletes (Cassandra TTL, S3 lifecycle, partition drops).
  • Crypto-shredding: encrypt each user's data with a per-user key; delete the key to make all copies, backups included, unreadable.
  • PCI-DSS for card data (use Stripe/Adyen tokens so card numbers never touch your servers), HIPAA for US health data.
-- retention by partition drop (cheap, vs row-by-row delete)
ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_2025_01;
DROP TABLE events_2025_01;
-- masked view for analysts
CREATE VIEW users_masked AS SELECT id, left(email,1)||'***@'||split_part(email,'@',2) AS email FROM users;

Worked example. 100M users, per-user encryption key (32 B) = 3.2 GB of keys in KMS/DB; deleting 10k users' keys per day makes their data in S3 logs and backups instantly unreadable, with no scanning of petabytes.

Industry examples. Stripe tokenises cards; Apple differential privacy; Uber and Airbnb run internal data catalogs that tag PII columns for automated deletion; log pipelines scrub emails and phone numbers via regex before indexing.

Decision gravity. The PII vault and tokenisation decision is cheap early, nearly impossible to undo after PII has spread to 40 services. Crypto-shredding must be designed in at write time.

Everyday analogy. Keeping passports in the hotel safe and giving staff a room number, not the passport copy.

Common interview traps.

  • Logging PII or tokens (log pipelines are rarely access-controlled like databases).
  • Using production data in test environments.
  • Believing hashing an email makes it anonymous (hashes of emails are easily reversed by guessing).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Expect abuse: volumetric DDoS, L7 floods, credential stuffing, scraping, fake accounts. Layer defences from CDN to app.
  • Rate limit with token bucket (burst plus average), atomic in Redis, keyed by IP + account + API key; return 429 with Retry-After; clients back off with jitter; decide fail-open or closed.
  • Shed low-priority load before collapse; keep critical paths reserved.
  • DDoS: anycast CDN/scrubbing, cache, lock the origin to the shield, redundant DNS, budget caps on autoscale.
  • WAF: managed rules, log-only first, virtual patching; a safety net not a fix.
  • Bots: score signals (reputation, behaviour, fingerprint), challenge in tiers, attest mobile apps, use waiting rooms and per-account limits.
  • Credential stuffing: per-account limits, breached-password checks, MFA/passkeys, uniform error messages.
  • GDPR: lawful basis, user rights (access, erasure, portability), minimisation, retention, 72-hour breach notice, residency. Design deletion across all copies.
  • PII: classify, isolate in a vault, tokenise, mask, audit, retention TTLs, crypto-shredding; never log it.
